messages.content: I want to develop a semantic parser that can handle variable binding and quantifier scope in combinations it has not seen before, without losing accuracy on familiar constructions. What should count as success?

There are two requirements. On withheld scope–binding combinations, with vocabulary and length distributions matched, the parser should achieve at least 90% logical-form exact match. On familiar constructions, its exact-match accuracy should remain within two percentage points of an equally sized supervised baseline. The goal is to meet both requirements, rather than improve generalization by giving up familiar-construction accuracy.
What makes this a test of composition rather than simply a test of unusual words or longer inputs?

The target is the combination of scope and binding phenomena that has been withheld, not unfamiliar vocabulary or greater length. Requiring matched vocabulary and length distributions is meant to keep those properties from being the obvious explanation for a difference in performance. It does not, by itself, say that every other property of the inputs is identical.
Could you unpack what scope and binding each contribute here?

Quantifier scope concerns how quantifiers are ordered in an interpretation: changing their relative scope can change what a statement means. Variable binding concerns which expressions introduce variables and which occurrences depend on them. A semantic parser needs to produce a logical form that captures those relationships. The challenge in this goal is to do so when scope and binding appear together in withheld combinations.
So seeing the relevant ingredients individually would not, by itself, satisfy the goal?

Right. The stated generalization target is unseen compositions. Recognizing familiar ingredients is not the same as producing the correct logical form when their scope–binding relationship appears in a withheld combination. The ≥90% exact-match requirement applies to those withheld combinations.
Why specify logical-form exact match instead of saying the output should be roughly semantically right?

Exact match sets a stricter target: the produced logical form must match the expected one under the evaluation's matching convention. A response that gestures toward the right interpretation but fails that match would not count. The goal does not specify a convention for treating differently written but equivalent logical forms, so it would be premature to assume how such cases are scored.
And the 90% figure is a floor, not just an aspiration to do reasonably well?

Yes. The requirement is at least 90% logical-form exact match on the withheld scope–binding combinations under the stated matched-distribution condition. A result below 90% would not meet that requirement, even if it represented an improvement over some other result.
Does the wording require 90% for every kind of withheld combination separately?

It specifies ≥90% exact match on withheld scope–binding combinations, but does not state a separate threshold for each subtype. We should preserve that stated target rather than add a per-subtype requirement or assume a particular way of grouping the combinations.
I also don't want the parser to become specialized for the withheld cases and worse on constructions it already handles. How is that captured?

That is the familiar-construction requirement. Its exact-match accuracy must stay within two percentage points of an equally sized supervised baseline. This makes familiar performance a condition of success alongside the ≥90% target on withheld scope–binding combinations.
What exactly does 'two percentage points' mean in that comparison?

It is a difference between accuracy percentages, not a relative percentage change. If the baseline's familiar-construction exact-match accuracy is B%, the stated comparison allows a gap of no more than two percentage points. The node does not give B or a measured parser accuracy.
Should we assume what 'equally sized' refers to or which supervised approach the baseline uses?

No. The requirement identifies an equally sized supervised baseline for the familiar-construction comparison, but does not give its architecture, training details, or the basis on which size is measured. Those details should not be filled in as though they were part of the goal.
Is matching vocabulary distributions the same thing as merely using a familiar vocabulary?

Not necessarily. 'Matched vocabulary and length distributions' is more specific than saying only that the words are familiar or that the inputs are not longer on average. The requirement names distributions for both properties. It does not specify a matching procedure, so the important point here is to retain that condition without inventing one.
If the parser reaches the withheld-combination threshold but familiar accuracy falls farther from the baseline than allowed, would that meet the overall goal?

No. The two requirements are simultaneous. Reaching at least 90% on withheld scope–binding combinations would address the generalization target, but familiar-construction exact-match accuracy would still need to be within two percentage points of the equally sized supervised baseline.
And strong familiar-construction accuracy alone would leave the main generalization question open?

Yes. Matching the baseline closely on familiar constructions would address retention of familiar accuracy, but it would not establish the required performance on withheld scope–binding combinations. The goal joins the two: generalize to those unseen compositions while maintaining familiar-construction accuracy within the stated comparison.
So the claim we are aiming to substantiate is quite precise, rather than a general claim that the parser is compositional?

Exactly. The stated target is a semantic parser for variable binding and quantifier scope that achieves ≥90% logical-form exact match on withheld scope–binding combinations with matched vocabulary and length distributions, while keeping familiar-construction exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of an equally sized supervised baseline. That is more specific than an unrestricted claim about all forms of compositional generalization.
For that goal, I propose training a typed de Bruijn-indexed grammar decoder on a fixed-size mix of synthetic scope–binding recombinations and original examples.

That is a concrete training proposal. The decoder would produce logical forms through a grammar with types and de Bruijn-style variable references, while its training mix would contain both synthetic recombinations of scope and binding and original examples. Calling the mix fixed-size specifies a constraint on its total size, but does not specify the number of examples or how that total is divided between the two sources.
Can you explain what the three parts of the decoder description mean without assuming a particular implementation?

A grammar decoder generates outputs according to a grammar rather than treating every output as an unconstrained string. 'Typed' indicates that type information is part of that output representation or its constraints. 'De Bruijn-indexed' describes a way of representing bound-variable references by their relation to binders rather than relying on arbitrary variable names. The proposal does not specify the grammar rules, the type system, or the decoder architecture.
Why would de Bruijn indexing be relevant to variable binding?

Binding is about which binder a variable occurrence refers to. De Bruijn indexing makes that relationship explicit in the representation, instead of depending on the particular names chosen for variables. That is why it is pertinent to this proposal. It remains a representational choice, though; the proposal does not establish that the parser will learn to use it correctly in unseen combinations.
And does 'typed' mean we're claiming the model will always produce a correct interpretation?

No. Type information can express restrictions on which parts of a logical form fit together, but satisfying such restrictions is not the same as choosing the intended quantifier scope or the correct binder for every occurrence. The proposal names a typed decoder; it makes no performance claim.
What does the grammar contribute as distinct from typing and indexing?

They describe different aspects of the proposed output process. The grammar describes the structural forms the decoder can build; typing concerns how components may fit together; de Bruijn indexing concerns how bound-variable references are represented. None of those labels, on its own, specifies the exact logical-form language or guarantees that a generated form matches the intended meaning.
When I say synthetic scope–binding recombinations, am I saying we need entirely new vocabulary?

No. The phrase points to recombining scope and binding patterns for training, not to introducing new words. It does not specify a synthesis procedure, the vocabulary of the resulting examples, or a particular distribution of lengths.
What is the role of the original examples in the mix?

The proposal retains original examples alongside the synthetic recombinations in training. That is consistent with attending to familiar constructions while exploring new combinations. It does not, however, assert that retaining them is sufficient to preserve familiar-construction accuracy; that remains something the parser would have to achieve.
Could 'fixed-size mix' be read as half synthetic and half original?
No. A fixed-size mix has a fixed total size and includes both kinds of examples, but the wording gives no proportion. An equal split would be an additional decision, not something already specified.
Does fixed-size refer to the decoder's size instead?

Here it modifies the mix of training examples, not the decoder. The proposal does not state a parameter count or another measure of model size. The equally sized supervised baseline in the goal is a separate comparison, so this phrase alone does not settle how model sizes would be matched.
Is this a claim that the synthetic examples already cover every withheld scope–binding combination?

No. The proposal says to train on synthetic scope–binding recombinations; it does not enumerate them or claim exhaustive coverage. Nor does it say that withheld evaluation combinations are included in training. Its purpose is to propose a way to train for generalization, not to report that generalization has occurred.
Could someone reasonably describe this as combining an output representation choice with a training-data choice?

Yes. A typed, de Bruijn-indexed grammar decoder describes the proposed output representation and decoding approach. A fixed-size mix of synthetic scope–binding recombinations and original examples describes the proposed training input. Keeping those parts distinct helps avoid treating either one as a demonstrated explanation for success.
I don't want the proposal to imply that synthetically recombining examples automatically solves quantifier scope.

It need not imply that. The recombinations are proposed training material; correct scope assignment in unseen compositions is still an ability the resulting semantic parser would need to demonstrate. Likewise, the typed grammar and de Bruijn indices describe how logical forms are represented and generated, not a guarantee that the intended logical form will be selected.
How should we describe the proposal in one sentence while preserving those distinctions?

Train a typed de Bruijn-indexed grammar decoder using a fixed-size training mix that includes synthetic scope–binding recombinations and original examples, as a proposed approach to generalizing scope and binding without giving up accuracy on familiar constructions.
Does that sentence commit us to a particular mixing ratio, generation algorithm, or result?

No. It states the decoder choice and the two kinds of training examples, with a fixed total mix size. It neither chooses a ratio or synthesis algorithm nor claims that either accuracy requirement has been met.
Does synthetic recombination improve binding across nested quantifiers without distorting scope choices in familiar constructions?

That is an open question, not an established effect of the proposed training mix. It asks whether synthetic recombination helps the parser identify which binder a variable depends on when quantifiers are nested, while leaving its scope choices for familiar constructions intact. Both parts matter: an improvement in binding would not, by itself, answer the concern about familiar scope choices.
What makes binding across nested quantifiers a particular concern?

With nested quantifiers, a variable occurrence may need to be associated with one binder rather than another. The parser must represent that dependency correctly even when several binders are in play. The question is whether exposure to synthetic recombinations helps with that distinction; it does not assert that it does.
Is that the same as choosing the right quantifier scope?

They are related but distinct. Binding concerns which binder a variable occurrence refers to. Scope concerns the relative reach or ordering of quantifiers in the interpretation. A logical form can represent variable references in a well-formed way and still choose a scope that does not match the intended reading. That is why the question names both binding improvement and possible distortion of scope choices.
What would 'distorting scope choices' mean here?

It would mean that training with synthetic recombinations changes the parser's scope decisions on familiar constructions in an undesirable way—for instance, selecting an interpretation that does not match the intended one where it otherwise would. The wording raises that possibility; it does not say that such a distortion has been observed.
So this isn't just asking whether synthetic examples produce grammatical logical forms?

Correct. Grammaticality alone would not settle either part of the question. A grammatical logical form could attach a variable to the wrong binder or express the wrong quantifier scope. The concern is whether the parser makes the intended binding and scope choices, particularly whether any gain in nested binding comes without a cost on familiar constructions.
Does the de Bruijn-indexed decoder make the binding part automatic?

No. De Bruijn indexing provides a way to express which binder a variable refers to, but the parser still has to choose the appropriate reference for the intended interpretation. A representation can make the distinction explicit without guaranteeing that the model selects correctly across nested quantifiers.
And a typed grammar wouldn't automatically protect familiar scope choices either?

Right. Typing and grammar constraints concern which logical forms can be constructed under the chosen representation. More than one scope choice may still be expressible. The open question is about which interpretation the trained parser actually favors on familiar constructions, not simply whether it can produce a structurally permitted form.
Am I implicitly assuming synthetic recombination is harmful to familiar constructions by asking this?

No. The wording leaves both outcomes open. Synthetic recombination might help binding across nested quantifiers without disturbing familiar scope choices, it might help one aspect but not the other, or it might not improve nested binding. The question asks whether the desired combination occurs; it does not presume a benefit or a cost.
Would better binding on recombined examples alone answer it?

Not fully. The question is about whether synthetic recombination improves binding across nested quantifiers and does so without distorting scope choices in familiar constructions. Evidence limited to binding on recombined material would leave the familiar-scope concern unanswered. Conversely, unchanged familiar scope choices alone would not establish improved nested binding.
Is the concern about a particular scope reading being preferred?

No particular reading is specified. The question does not designate one quantifier ordering as universally correct, nor does it give a particular familiar construction and its intended logical form. It asks more generally whether scope decisions for familiar constructions remain appropriate rather than being pulled toward an unintended choice.
Could 'improve binding' just mean that the output contains variable references more often?

That would be too weak a reading. The binding concern is whether variable occurrences refer to the appropriate binders across nested quantifiers. Merely including references—or producing a formally valid reference—would not necessarily capture the intended binding relationship.
What is the most careful short statement of the issue?

Whether training with synthetic scope–binding recombinations helps the parser assign variables to the right binders under nested quantifiers, while preserving appropriate quantifier-scope choices on familiar constructions, remains an open question.

My hypothesis is that a 1:1 synthetic–original mix will yield at least 90% exact match on withheld scope–binding combinations, with no more than a two-percentage-point loss in familiar-construction accuracy versus equal-sized supervision.

That is a prediction about both sides of the question: performance on withheld scope–binding combinations and retention of accuracy on familiar constructions. The 1:1 ratio specifies equal amounts of synthetic recombinations and original examples in the training mix. The ≥90% withheld exact-match result and ≤2-point familiar accuracy loss are hypothesized outcomes, not results already observed.
Does the 1:1 ratio say how many training examples there are?

No. It specifies the balance between synthetic and original examples, not the total count. In the proposed fixed-size mix, the two sources would contribute equally, but no numerical size is stated here.
Why is it important to state the familiar-accuracy condition alongside the withheld-combination target?

Because success on withheld combinations alone would not establish that familiar constructions remain well handled. The hypothesis predicts both ≥90% exact match on the withheld scope–binding combinations and a familiar-construction accuracy loss of no more than two percentage points relative to equal-sized supervision. It is the conjunction of those predicted outcomes that addresses the concern about gaining generalization at the expense of familiar performance.
When you say a two-point loss, do you mean two percent of the baseline's accuracy?

No. A two-percentage-point loss is an absolute difference between accuracy percentages, not a relative reduction of two percent. The hypothesis permits at most that much decline in familiar-construction accuracy compared with equal-sized supervision; it does not give either accuracy as a measured value.
Is 'no more than a two-point loss' the same as predicting that familiar accuracy will be exactly two points lower?
No. It sets a maximum allowed loss. The hypothesis also accommodates a smaller loss or no loss. It does not predict an exact familiar-construction accuracy figure.
What does the withheld exact-match prediction say about binding across nested quantifiers?

It predicts strong exact-match performance on withheld scope–binding combinations, which is relevant to the question of generalizing binding and scope together. But the hypothesis states an aggregate threshold for those combinations; it does not separately state a numerical result for binding specifically across nested quantifiers. We should not turn the ≥90% figure into an unstated binding-only guarantee.
Likewise, does a small loss on familiar constructions prove that their scope choices have not changed?

Not by itself. Familiar-construction exact-match accuracy is an overall measure of whether the predicted logical forms match the expected ones. A loss of no more than two percentage points would support the stated accuracy condition, but that aggregate number alone would not describe every individual scope choice. The hypothesis addresses the concern about familiar performance without asserting that no familiar scope decision ever changes.
So this hypothesis relates to the earlier question, but doesn't claim to have answered it already?

Exactly. It offers a testable prediction relevant to whether synthetic recombination can help with withheld scope–binding compositions without appreciably harming familiar accuracy. It does not report an experiment or establish that nested binding improves or that familiar scope choices are unaffected.
Could we phrase the prediction without implying the typed decoder or the 1:1 mix is guaranteed to work?

Yes: 'We hypothesize that training with a 1:1 mix of synthetic scope–binding recombinations and original examples will achieve ≥90% exact match on withheld scope–binding combinations, while familiar-construction accuracy falls by no more than two percentage points relative to equal-sized supervision.' That preserves the predicted thresholds without presenting them as findings.
Does 'equal-sized supervision' mean the comparison is against the synthetic examples alone?

No. It denotes an equally sized supervised comparison for familiar-construction accuracy. The synthetic–original split describes the proposed training mix; it is not itself the familiar-accuracy baseline. The hypothesis does not specify further details of the supervised comparison.
Would hitting the 90% threshold but losing more than two points on familiar constructions support the whole hypothesis?
No. The hypothesis predicts both conditions together. Meeting the withheld exact-match threshold while exceeding the permitted familiar-accuracy loss would fall short of the joint prediction.
And if familiar accuracy stays close to supervision but withheld exact match is below 90%?
That would also fall short of the joint prediction. Retaining familiar accuracy would not substitute for reaching ≥90% exact match on the withheld scope–binding combinations.
I want to be careful about what the hypothesis does not specify. Does it name a particular way to synthesize the recombinations?

No. It specifies a 1:1 synthetic–original training mix and predicts two performance conditions. It does not supply a synthesis algorithm, a total example count, or results for individual scope or binding subcategories.
Then the central claim remains a proposed outcome of that training balance, rather than a statement that we have already seen it happen?

Yes. The 1:1 balance is the proposed condition, and ≥90% withheld scope–binding exact match together with ≤2-percentage-point familiar accuracy loss versus equal-sized supervision is the hypothesized outcome.
How should we plan the comparison so it addresses whether synthetic recombination helps with scope and binding without sacrificing familiar constructions?

Build withheld scope–binding splits matched for vocabulary and length, train a mixed decoder and a supervised decoder of equal size, and compare their logical-form exact match on both familiar constructions and the withheld splits. That sets up the two comparisons the question needs. It is a plan for evaluation, not a report of how either decoder performs.
What is being withheld in those splits?

The withheld aspect is the scope–binding combinations. The point is to examine performance on those combinations rather than attribute a difference simply to different vocabulary or input lengths. The plan does not specify the individual combinations or a procedure for constructing the splits.
Does matching vocabulary and length mean the sentences in the splits have to be identical?

No. Matching those properties does not mean using identical sentences; identical sentences would not test withheld combinations. The plan calls for vocabulary- and length-matched splits while preserving the distinction between the scope–binding combinations being evaluated. It does not define an exact matching method.
And 'equal-sized' applies to the decoders, correct?

Yes. The plan says to train equal-sized mixed and supervised decoders. It does not, by that wording alone, specify identical training-example counts, the size measure used for the decoders, or every other training detail.
What distinguishes the mixed decoder from the supervised one in this plan?

The mixed decoder is the one trained using the proposed mix of synthetic scope–binding recombinations and original examples. The supervised decoder provides the comparison trained with supervision. The plan does not add a mixing ratio or detailed training specification; its explicit comparison is between equal-sized decoders evaluated on familiar and withheld exact match.
Why compare them on both familiar and withheld examples instead of just the withheld splits?

Withheld exact match addresses generalization to the scope–binding combinations of interest. Familiar exact match addresses the separate concern that training with recombinations might affect performance on constructions already represented in the original examples. Looking at only the withheld side would leave that familiar-construction concern unanswered.
Would strong familiar exact match alone settle whether recombination helps binding across nested quantifiers?

No. Familiar performance speaks to retention of accuracy on familiar constructions. The withheld comparison is needed to examine generalization. Even then, overall exact match on withheld scope–binding combinations should not automatically be described as a separate measurement of binding across nested quantifiers unless the evaluated cases and results support that narrower statement.
Likewise, if the mixed decoder has higher withheld exact match, can we immediately say its scope choices on familiar constructions are unchanged?

No. Higher withheld exact match would say something about that comparison on the withheld splits, not about familiar scope choices. Comparing familiar exact match is the part of the plan that bears on familiar performance, although an aggregate familiar score alone would not show that every individual scope choice stayed the same.
What does exact match contribute to the comparison?

It asks whether a decoder's predicted logical form matches the expected logical form, rather than merely whether its output looks plausible or well formed. Applying that measure to both decoders on familiar and withheld cases gives a direct comparison on the two kinds of constructions. The plan does not specify the matching convention for differently written but equivalent forms.
Is the plan already a finding that the mixed decoder beats supervision?

No. Building the splits, training the decoders, and comparing their exact match are proposed actions. The plan states neither decoder's score and does not conclude that the mixed decoder improves withheld performance or preserves familiar performance.
Could the comparison still be informative if the two decoders do differently on familiar and withheld cases?

Yes. That contrast is precisely why the plan includes both evaluations. Differences on the withheld splits and differences on familiar constructions bear on different parts of the question. What those differences actually are, and whether they satisfy any desired performance conditions, remains unknown until the comparison is made.
Does the plan require us to claim that matching vocabulary and length removes every possible confound?

No. It specifically calls for matching vocabulary and length in the withheld scope–binding splits. That makes those two properties less likely to account for a performance difference, but the plan does not claim that every other difference has been eliminated.
Can you state the sequence of planned work without turning it into an experiment we've already run?

First, build the vocabulary- and length-matched withheld scope–binding splits. Then train the equal-sized mixed and supervised decoders. Finally, compare their logical-form exact match on familiar constructions and on the withheld splits. Each step is prospective; no results are specified.
So the comparison is meant to inform the question about nested binding and familiar scope, but we should keep its conclusions tied to what we actually measure?

Exactly. The plan addresses that question by comparing performance on withheld scope–binding combinations and familiar constructions under an equal-decoder-size comparison. Any later claim specifically about binding across nested quantifiers or particular familiar scope choices would need to stay within what the evaluated cases and exact-match results actually show.

For the split-building activity, I want to construct ScopeBind-v1 splits that withhold nested-quantifier/binding pairings while matching vocabulary and the length distributions of both utterances and logical forms.

That specifies what ScopeBind-v1 is intended to test and what the splits should keep comparable. The withheld feature is the pairing of nested-quantifier structure with binding, while vocabulary, utterance-length distributions, and logical-form-length distributions are to be matched. This describes a construction activity; it does not say that the splits have already been built.
When you say the pairings are withheld, does that mean nested quantifiers are absent altogether?

No. Withholding nested-quantifier/binding pairings is not the same as excluding every instance of nested quantification or every instance of binding. The distinction being targeted is how those features occur together. The activity does not specify exactly which instances of either feature appear elsewhere in the splits.
Why call out the pairing rather than just say we're withholding difficult logical forms?

Because the pairing identifies the compositional distinction of interest. 'Difficult logical forms' would be too broad: it would not say whether the withheld material concerns nested quantifiers, binding, their combination, or something else. ScopeBind-v1 is described specifically in terms of nested-quantifier/binding pairings.
Does matching vocabulary mean every utterance must use exactly the same words as another utterance?

No. Vocabulary matching is a property of the splits, not a requirement that individual utterances be word-for-word identical. The activity does not specify whether matching is implemented through shared word types, a frequency criterion, or some other procedure, so we should not assume one.
I want to be explicit that length matching applies on both sides of the parsing task.

Yes. The activity names utterance length and logical-form length separately. Matching only the lengths of input utterances would leave the stated logical-form-length condition unaddressed; matching only logical-form lengths would leave the utterance-length condition unaddressed.
Is matching a length distribution stronger than saying the average lengths happen to be similar?

Generally, yes. A distribution describes how lengths are spread across examples, whereas an average is only one summary of that spread. The activity calls for matching utterance- and logical-form-length distributions, not merely reporting similar averages. It does not specify a numerical tolerance or a particular test for matching.
Why pay attention to logical-form length as well as utterance length?

Logical-form length is a property of the target output. If the withheld material systematically differed in output length, performance differences could be harder to interpret as differences specifically associated with the withheld pairings. Matching its length distribution alongside utterance length is intended to keep both named length properties comparable; it does not guarantee that all other properties are comparable.
Would those matching conditions make the withheld combinations no longer withheld?

No. The matching conditions concern vocabulary and the two length distributions. The withholding condition concerns nested-quantifier/binding pairings. Examples can be comparable in those named surface and output-length properties while differing in the pairing being tested.
Should 'ScopeBind-v1' be treated as evidence that a previous split or a later version exists?
No. ScopeBind-v1 is the name given to these proposed splits. The name alone does not establish that any other version exists, nor does it report a completed construction or evaluation.
What exactly are we committing to matching across the splits?

The stated commitments are vocabulary, the distribution of utterance lengths, and the distribution of logical-form lengths. No additional matching variables, matching algorithm, split sizes, or numerical tolerances are specified.
Is it fair to say that the vocabulary condition is there so the test isn't simply about unfamiliar words?

That is a fair explanation of its relevance. Matching vocabulary helps keep a vocabulary difference from being the obvious reason for a performance difference. It should not be stretched into a claim that every lexical property is controlled or that vocabulary matching alone isolates the effect of the withheld pairings.
Does the activity prescribe a particular formalism for measuring logical-form length?

No. It says to match logical-form length distributions, but does not define a length unit or counting convention. The important point in this description is that target lengths are included in the matching condition, not that a particular measurement procedure has already been chosen.
Are we claiming these splits will by themselves show whether synthetic recombination works?

No. Constructing ScopeBind-v1 splits creates the intended withheld-combination evaluation setting. The activity contains no trained-decoder results and no conclusion about the effect of synthetic recombination. A split can support a comparison without itself supplying the outcome.
Could someone misread 'withholding nested-quantifier/binding pairings' as withholding only long utterances?

That would miss the distinction. The withholding is defined by the pairing of nested quantification and binding, not by utterance length. In fact, utterance-length distributions are among the properties to match, along with vocabulary and logical-form-length distributions.
Nor does the phrase tell us the exact number of splits or their sizes, right?

Right. 'Splits' identifies the construction to be made, but the activity does not provide a count of examples, a count of withheld pairings, or sizes for the resulting partitions. Those details should not be supplied as though they were already specified.
Can you restate the activity without turning it into a result?

Construct ScopeBind-v1 splits that withhold nested-quantifier/binding pairings, while matching vocabulary across the splits and matching the distributions of both utterance lengths and logical-form lengths. This states the intended construction conditions, not that the splits are complete or that a parser has achieved any particular accuracy on them.
What does ScopeBind-v1 contain?

ScopeBind-v1 contains a training split, a familiar-test split, and a withheld-pairing test split. It also includes vocabulary and length-matching audit tables. Those are the components specified for the artifact; no example counts or evaluation scores are given.
Why have two test splits rather than just one?

They serve different comparisons. The familiar-test split is for evaluating familiar constructions, while the withheld-pairing test split is for evaluating the scope–binding pairings held out for that test. Keeping them distinct makes it possible to discuss familiar performance and performance on withheld compositions separately.
Does 'withheld-pairing' refer to withholding words?

No. The pairings in question are nested-quantifier/binding pairings. Vocabulary is a separate property covered by the matching audit tables. The withheld-pairing label should not be read as saying that the test is about unfamiliar words.
What role does the training split play in describing the artifact?

It identifies the training portion of ScopeBind-v1, distinct from the two test portions. The artifact description does not specify its size, list its examples, or say that any decoder has already been trained on it.
Can we infer from the training split that it contains the 1:1 synthetic–original mix?

No. A 1:1 mix is a training hypothesis discussed separately. The description of ScopeBind-v1 says that it contains a training split, but does not state the composition of that split or how a later training mix would be assembled.
What do the audit tables add beyond naming the splits?

They provide a place to inspect the vocabulary and length-matching properties associated with the splits. That matters because the withheld-pairing distinction is easier to interpret when the named vocabulary and length properties can also be examined. The artifact description does not supply the tables' entries or a numerical conclusion from them.
Which lengths are relevant here?

The ScopeBind-v1 split construction calls out both utterance-length and logical-form-length distributions. Accordingly, 'length-matching' here concerns the input utterances and the target logical forms, not just one side of the parsing task.
Does having length-matching audit tables mean we already know the distributions match perfectly?

Not from this description alone. It says the audit tables are included, but gives neither their values nor a pass-or-fail judgment. Their presence should not be turned into a claim of perfect matching or a particular tolerance.
And the vocabulary audit tables aren't themselves a parser evaluation, are they?

Right. Vocabulary and length-matching audits concern properties of the splits. Parser evaluation would concern predicted logical forms on examples in the test splits. The artifact description includes audit tables, but reports no parser predictions or exact-match accuracy.
If someone quotes a score for ScopeBind-v1 familiar-test from this description, would that be supported?

No. Familiar-test is named as a component of ScopeBind-v1, but no decoder result or familiar-test score is stated. The same applies to the withheld-pairing test split: its existence is specified, not an accuracy on it.
Does the withheld-pairing test split specify every individual pairing it contains?

No. Its name identifies its purpose, and the split construction identifies nested-quantifier/binding pairings as the withheld feature. Neither statement enumerates the particular pairings or examples in that test split.
Could the familiar-test and withheld-pairing test splits have different numbers of examples?
The description gives no sizes, so it does not establish whether their example counts are equal or different. We can identify their distinct roles without assuming a numerical balance between them.
Is there any reason to keep the audit tables conceptually separate from the test splits?

Yes. The test splits identify which examples are used for the familiar and withheld-pairing evaluations. The audit tables concern comparability of vocabulary and lengths. A table about split properties is not itself another test split, and a test split's existence does not state the outcome of its audit.
How would you describe ScopeBind-v1 in one careful sentence?
ScopeBind-v1 is an artifact containing training, familiar-test, and withheld-pairing test splits, together with vocabulary and length-matching audit tables.
And that sentence deliberately stops short of saying whether the parser meets the exact-match targets?

Yes. It describes what the artifact contains. It makes no claim that a parser has been evaluated, achieved the withheld-pairing exact-match target, or maintained familiar-construction accuracy relative to a supervised comparison.
Now that ScopeBind-v1 has its splits and audit tables, what activity will evaluate the training hypothesis?

Audit ScopeBind-v1 for vocabulary and length matching, train equal-sized mixed and supervised decoders, and compare their logical-form exact match on the withheld-pairing and familiar-test splits against the stated thresholds. This describes the work to do; it does not report audit findings, trained models, or accuracy results.
What exactly should the audit cover?

It should examine vocabulary matching and the length distributions for both utterances and logical forms. ScopeBind-v1 includes audit tables for vocabulary and length matching, but their presence alone does not establish that the matching conditions have been met.
Why do that audit as part of the evaluation activity rather than go straight to accuracy?

The withheld-pairing comparison is intended to focus on scope–binding composition. Checking the named matching conditions helps us interpret that comparison without simply assuming that vocabulary or input and output lengths are comparable. The audit does not, by itself, tell us how either decoder performs.
Does the audit require the two test splits to contain identical utterances or logical forms?

No. It concerns the stated vocabulary and length properties, not identity of examples. The familiar-test and withheld-pairing test splits have different evaluation roles; the activity does not specify an audit procedure or require example-by-example identity.
After the audit, what are we training?
